description: We are NarSpot, Mohammed and Mansour, a Dubai team taking on Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. Our project, FireBridge, will join 24 years of NASA fire satellite records into one consistent burning calendar that also shows when satellites could not see the ground. We bring Python, web development, AI-assisted coding, pitching and storytelling. We welcome teammates with GIS, remote sensing or data science skills, or UI design.
summary:
FireBridge is a web application that turns NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one consistent fire history people can trust. The two satellite instruments count fire very differently: VIIRS detects 5 to 8 times more, so simply joining their records creates a false jump in 2012. FireBridge harmonizes both sensors into a single unit, using a calibration chosen by pre-registered rules and tested on years and regions it never saw.

Users can view MODIS, VIIRS or both on a 3D globe, maps, a calendar heatmap and a table, all synchronized to one date and region selection. Uniquely, FireBridge marks days when satellites were offline as “unavailable” instead of showing them as zero fire. It also forecasts next-day detections with a tested AI model, and connects any hotspot to verified emergency contacts.

This matters now: the Suomi NPP satellite stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026, and fire services need a reliable baseline to judge whether fire activity is unusual.
details:
What it does and how it works

FireBridge turns NASA’s satellite fire detections into one fire history that people can trust. NASA records fire with two instruments: MODIS (Terra and Aqua satellites, since 2000) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, since 2012). VIIRS has finer resolution and detects 5 to 8 times more fire, so simply joining the records creates a false jump. In Argentina, the naive record jumps almost 4 times in 2012, although nothing changed on the ground.

FireBridge works in four steps:

  1. Harmonize. Detections are counted on NASA’s 0.25° grid, and VIIRS counts are converted to MODIS-equivalent units using a calibration fitted where both satellites overlapped (2012–2017). We compared five conversion methods under rules written before testing, and ran the final test only once.
  2. Verify. Every day is checked against NASA’s official FIRMS outage records. Days without coverage are shown as “unavailable”, never as zero fire.
  3. Explore. Users switch between Combined, MODIS and VIIRS views on a 3D globe, 2D maps, a calendar heatmap and a data table. One shared date, region and filter selection keeps every view in sync, and a Debug Portal shows MODIS and VIIRS maps side by side.
  4. Act. Clicking a hotspot shows its coordinates, nearby detections, a next-day estimate from our AI model, and official emergency contacts verified on government websites.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Emergency responders can tell whether a quiet period is real or just missing data.
  • Fire services get a consistent baseline now that Suomi NPP has stopped delivering data (2 November 2026).
  • Scientists and land managers get comparable fire records from 2002 onward, with every number traceable to NASA.

Tools and technologies

  • Python: pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, SciPy, Flask, remotezip.
  • JavaScript: three.js (3D globe), D3.js (maps and charts), topojson-client, SheetJS (Excel export).
  • HTML/CSS, GitHub Pages for hosting, and a small Flask backend that keeps the FIRMS API key server-side, splits requests into 5-day chunks, caches responses and retries failures.
  • No special hardware: everything runs on a laptop.

What makes it creative
Most fire maps only show where fire was seen. FireBridge also shows where the satellites could not see, and says “can’t tell” when the data doesn’t support an answer. Our team name carries the idea: “Nar” means fire in Arabic, and we spot it from space.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: we pre-registered our test rules, held out both years and regions, and report every result, including failures. For example, our interval coverage for unseen regions was 65%, below our 70% target.
  • Data integrity: each record keeps its satellite, UTC timestamp and original confidence value. MODIS and VIIRS confidence scales are never forced into one scale, and missing values stay missing.
  • Model evaluation: the next-day forecast was tested on 2022–2024 data it never saw. It scored AUC 0.78, against 0.67 for a simple persistence rule, and 0.80 in regions excluded from training.
  • Safety: satellite detections are labelled as thermal anomalies, not confirmed fires. FireBridge never contacts authorities automatically, and it shows only contacts verified on official sites.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes, text labels on every badge, keyboard navigation and phone-friendly layouts.
  • Known limitations: cloud cover is not yet included, the AI model covers three regions (Argentina, California and Kalimantan), and the FIRMS area API needs a free key that we couldn’t test with a real key during the event.
